_note: Baseline INHERENT-EXPOSURE starting points by sector, as a scaffold for the assessor. Grounded in the risk framing of NIST SP 800-82, the NIST CSF, and the consequence-driven approach of IEC 62443-3-2, plus practitioner judgement. These are starting points the assessor confirms or overrides, NOT determinations. Geopolitical/threat modifiers are applied on top by the assessor.

sectors.name: Water / wastewater
sectors.note: The sector is an essential service with safety-relevant treatment chemistry. It is increasingly targeted, and a compromise can affect public health.

sectors.name: Electricity transmission / distribution
sectors.note: The grid is critical national infrastructure with credible state-level targeting, such as Industroyer. A compromise has systemic and safety consequences.

sectors.name: Oil & gas
sectors.note: The sector is critical national infrastructure where process safety is at stake. It is a high-value target, including for state actors.

sectors.name: Nuclear
sectors.note: The sector is safety-critical to the highest degree and heavily regulated, and advanced attackers credibly target it.

sectors.name: Discrete manufacturing
sectors.note: The consequence is mainly operational and financial. Targeted risk varies with the product and IP, and ransomware is a common threat.

sectors.name: Process manufacturing (chemicals, etc.)
sectors.note: Process-safety consequence raises this above discrete manufacturing.

sectors.name: Food & beverage
sectors.note: The consequence is mainly to operations and supply continuity, with some safety exposure. The sector is heavily targeted by ransomware.

sectors.name: Rail
sectors.note: Rail is an essential service with safety-relevant systems, regulated under NIS and the CAF. A compromise has operational and safety consequences.

sectors.name: Aviation
sectors.note: Aviation is safety-critical and regulated by the CAA under the CAF for Aviation, and it attracts targeted interest from attackers.

sectors.name: Maritime / ports
sectors.note: Ports are an essential service, and a compromise has systemic economic consequences. Targeted interest is growing.

sectors.name: Healthcare / medical
sectors.note: Safety of life is at stake, the sector is regulated, and ransomware targets it heavily.

sectors.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturing
sectors.note: Process safety and high-value IP are both at stake. The sector is targeted and exposed to ransomware.

sectors.name: Data centre / digital infrastructure
sectors.note: Many other organisations depend on it, it is in scope of NIS2, and loss of availability has a high consequence.

sectors.name: Building management / smart building
sectors.note: The consequence is usually to operations and comfort. It rises where life-safety systems are integrated.

sectors.name: Other / not listed
sectors.note: This is a neutral starting point. Set the band from the organisation's criticality and consequence.

exposureModifiers.label: Operates in or serves a geopolitically exposed region or contested sector
Compromise has direct safety-of-life or major environmental consequence
Designated CNI / essential service / NIS2 essential entity
Many others depend on this organisation (single point of systemic failure)
Highly interconnected / large external attack surface
A compromise would be contained and have no safety consequence

hardRules: Baselines and modifiers scaffold the assessor's judgement; the assessor sets and can override the final exposure band.
Geopolitical judgements are the assessor's to make and record; the tool prompts but never asserts a geopolitical position on its own.
Safety-of-life consequence should not sit below 'high' without an explicit, recorded justification.
